title: One thing
hook: research on multitasking finds switching costs attention and time

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was burnout, and Elijah asleep under a tree until an angel said arise and eat. Your line was arise and eat. Today, something smaller than a break: one task at a time.

An email, half written, on the screen. A message pings, so you answer it. A tab with a news story. Back to the email: where was I? A calendar reminder. Back again. At the end of the hour, everything has been touched and nothing is finished. It felt like doing several things at once. The research on task switching suggests you weren't. You were doing one thing at a time, very fast, and paying a toll at every switch. Today: one thing.
screen: `AN EMAIL, A PING, A TAB.` → `WHERE WAS I?` → `A TOLL AT EVERY SWITCH.`

segments.voice: First, the research. In studies of task switching, such as work by Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans, people were slower when they had to switch between tasks than when they stayed with one, and the cost grew as the tasks got more complex. The mind has to drop one set of rules and pick up another, and that takes time and attention, even when it feels instant. Second, a very old line. Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible, says, "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." Not with half your might while checking something else. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes is blunt about how short life is, and this is part of his answer: give the thing in front of you your whole self. Third, a philosopher's version. The Danish thinker Søren Kierkegaard wrote a work known in English as Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. For him it went deeper than time management: a divided heart, wanting many things at once, can't fully want anything. One thing at a time, done with a whole heart, became for him a spiritual matter. Fourth, looking back at this week. Ruskin asked for joy in making. Morris asked for useful work. Gibran called work love made visible. Levin found the scythe moving on its own. A psychologist named flow. Elijah slept. Each, in its own way, asks for a person present to the thing in front of them, even when that thing is sleep: not doing less, but doing one thing, wholly, and then the next.
screen: `A TOLL AT EVERY SWITCH.` · `DO IT WITH THY MIGHT.` · `TO WILL ONE THING.` · `THE THREAD THROUGH THE WEEK.` · then, large: `ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing and stay with it: the feeling of your breath at the tip of your nose. When your attention switches, to a sound, a plan, an itch, you'll feel the little toll; no need to scold yourself, just switch back, and if you like, count each return on a finger. The point isn't a perfect score; it's practicing the way back.
One thing. Giving a single task your whole attention, because every switch has a cost, and a whole heart can only be given whole. Today's word.
Your line: practicing the way back. Every return counts, however many it takes. That's day nine hundred ten.

howItsDone: People who practice single-tasking often set a fixed block of time, close other windows and silence their phones; some also treat it as a form of mindfulness, returning gently whenever attention wanders.
